turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit. Before the doctor calls you, I'll grab the numbers. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point four, oxygen ninety-eight percent. You're looking comfortable.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I'm fine. Whole thing's a waste of a morning, hey.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't start. You were scratching the whole way from that robot by Checkers.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. I'm Doctor Naidoo. What brings you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, it's nothing. Just a little itch. She dragged me.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's a rash, Doc. He's been covered since the weekend, arms, chest, even a bit on the neck, scratching the whole time.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the neck. A few spots on the arms and the chest, that's it. I hardly notice.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Itchy spots on the arms and chest, and you're playing it down. When did you first notice them?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, two days. I nearly said Monday, but actually Wednesday, so two days. Already fading, honestly.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Saturday, after the braai. I saw the spots Sunday morning. That's four days, nearly five.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, not five days. Two days. And it's not sore, just a tiny bit itchy.

[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the timing is muddy, somewhere between two days and nearly five, and I'll hold that loosely for now. Talk me through the food, the cream, and the antibiotic, because any one of them could fit.

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, could be any of them, I don't actually know. Prawns at my cousin's braai, a new cream from the chemist for dry skin, and antibiotics from the clinic for a sinus thing. Or none of them. It's mild.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): One at a time, or we'll talk in circles. Which antibiotic, what dose, and are you still on it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, by mouth. I took it for two days and I stopped yesterday, because maybe that was it. So I'm off it.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did stop, I put the box in the cupboard. The sinus was already better before the pills, though. I don't know why he bothered.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't totally better. Mostly gone, but I still had a blocked nose, so I took them. It's fine now. Nothing left.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the cream, what's it called, and where do you put it?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Epimax, the pump bottle. Twice a day on my arms, for about a week. Still using it. Dry skin from the winter, nothing serious.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Morning and night, after his shower, ja. That bottle's nearly finished, he's been generous with it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, leave the bottle alone. I've got to fetch the bakkie from the garage before they close, so can we move?
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll move. The prawns, have you had them before without trouble?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Plenty of times, never a problem. Saturday was just a big plate, very lekker. I don't think it was the prawns, but I also can't say for sure.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines? Penicillin, or anything else?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Not medicine, not food, nothing.

[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not true. When he was small he got penicillin and came out in an itchy rash, same sort of thing. Our mother said so, and she's kept him off it ever since. Childhood.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No ways. That was my brother, not me. I have never had a penicillin allergy. She always mixes us up.

[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll note your sister remembers a childhood itchy rash with penicillin and you say that was your brother. I can't call it a confirmed allergy, and I won't ignore it either. We simply won't reach for penicillin-type antibiotics casually.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, whatever. I take Panado sometimes for a headache. Two tablets when I need them. Not often.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Panado now and then is fine. I'm not going to run through your whole history, the rash is what we're here for.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, good. Only thing I've ever had done is a wisdom tooth out, years ago. Doesn't matter.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He still tells that story like it was major surgery. It was one tooth.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): It was nothing. Can we stick to the itch, please? The garage closes at four.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the skin. A few faint pink patches on the forearms and upper chest, plus some scratch marks, and nothing on the neck. No swelling of the lips or the eyelids. Chest is clear, no wheeze.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Faint. I said it's nothing. Shirt back on?

[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ja, shirt on. Thinking aloud, I've got an itchy rash a few days old and three possible triggers sitting side by side, the prawns, the Epimax, and the amoxicillin, and I cannot tell which one did this. It does not look severe. No firm diagnosis from me today.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you won't even say it's the penicillin? Shame. I was sure.

[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so it stays on the list, but the cream can irritate dry skin and shellfish can do this even after years of being fine. Three possibilities, no winner.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So what now? I don't want a pile of tests. I'm not that sick.

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two things I weigh up: a non-sedating antihistamine for the itch, or a patch test to see if the cream is a contact problem. We'll start cetirizine, ten milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for seven days. The patch test only if this is not settling.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Cetirizine, fine. One a day. I can do that.

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop the Epimax for now, don't restart the amoxicillin, and leave the prawns alone until this has settled. If your tongue swells or you battle to breathe, go to casualty, not here.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, ja. Casualty if I can't breathe. I'm not going to stop breathing. This is over the top.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll try to make sure he stops the cream. He doesn't listen, but I'll try. Must I book a follow-up?
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it is not better in a week, come back and see me, and then we arrange the patch test. If it fades, stay home. No blood tests today. They wouldn't change what we do.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A week, sharp. If I'm fine I'm not coming, just so you know.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to poke in, Doctor. Next patient is waiting and this room is booked tight. Just a heads-up.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks, nearly done. Any tummy pain, vomiting, fever? Just making sure nothing else is sitting underneath.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever, no vomiting, tummy's fine. I told you I'm well.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting that I've seen, and he ate a full breakfast, so the tummy's not the issue. He'll still say he's well if he isn't, but on that he's right.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Mild rash, clear lungs, and I am not diagnosing a drug allergy today. Cetirizine as discussed, cream on hold, and you come back only if it's still there in a week. I've sent the script through.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Cetirizine, stop the cream, no amoxicillin, no prawns. If I'm still itchy in a week I'll come. Can we go now?
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja, before the garage shuts. Thank you, Doc. I'll keep an eye, even if he hates it.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pleasure. Don't let anyone give you another penicillin unless a doctor has heard this whole story. Off you go.
[SEG0055] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you to the front. Mind the step, it's loose. The script should be at the chemist counter downstairs, now-now.
